name: ARC (AI2 Reasoning Challenge)
description: The AI2 Reasoning Challenge (ARC) is a question set, text corpus, and baselines assembled to encourage AI research in advanced question answering. The ARC question set contains 7,787 natural, grade-school science questions (authored for human tests) partitioned into a Challenge Set (2,590 questions answered incorrectly by both a retrieval-based algorithm and a word co-occurrence algorithm) and an Easy Set (5,197 questions). The dataset also includes the ARC Corpus, a corpus of 14M science sentences relevant to the task, and implementations of three neural baseline models (DecompAttn, BiDAF, and DGEM).
creator: Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence (AI2)
citeAs: Clark, P., Cowhey, I., Etzioni, O., Khot, T., Sabharwal, A., Schoenick, C., & Tafjord, O. (2018). Think you have Solved Question Answering? Try ARC, the AI2 Reasoning Challenge. arXiv:1803.05457v1 [cs.AI].
rai:dataCollection: The ARC dataset was assembled through several months of extensive search and investigation to collect natural science questions authored for use on standardized tests. Questions were drawn from a variety of public-domain sources including state and national standardized tests (e.g., ACTAAP, AIMS, NAEP, NY Regents, TIMSS, etc.) as well as an anonymous content partner. The ARC Corpus was created by utilizing a major search engine to run a large series of search queries relevant to science, with queries automatically constructed by instantiating approximately 100 hand-written templates for 80 science topics covered by US elementary and middle schools.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Document analysis, Secondary Data analysis
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Natural science questions authored for use on standardized tests, drawn from a variety of sources including Arkansas Comprehensive Testing (ACTAAP), Arizona's Instrument to Measure Standards (AIMS), Alaska Department of Education, Florida Comprehensive Assessment Test (FCAT), NAEP, NY Regents exams, TIMSS assessments, and other state/national standardized tests. The ARC Corpus was sourced from web documents retrieved via a major search engine using science-related queries, augmented with the AristoMini corpus (dictionary definitions from Wiktionary, Simple Wikipedia science articles, and additional science sentences from the Web).
rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: Several months of extensive search and investigation prior to March 2018 (exact start date not specified).
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Questions were partitioned into a Challenge Set and an Easy Set based on whether both a retrieval-based (IR) algorithm and a word co-occurrence (PMI) algorithm answered them incorrectly. The Challenge Set contains 2,590 questions answered incorrectly by both algorithms; the Easy Set contains the remaining 5,197 questions. The ARC Corpus documents were de-duplicated, stripped down to text content, and chunked into sentences. The corpus was augmented with the AristoMini corpus.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For the ARC Corpus: top documents from each search query were collected and de-duplicated; document content was stripped to capture just the text; text was chunked into sentences. For baseline entailment models: questions were converted to Fill-In-The-Blank (FITB) statements, wh-words replaced with blanks, common multiple-choice phrases dropped, and answer choices inserted to generate hypothesis assertions. Long sentences (>300 characters), sentences with negation, and noisy sentences were filtered from retrieved sentences. Top 8 sentences based on ElasticSearch score were selected as candidate premises.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Questions were authored by human examiners for standardized tests (not annotated by the dataset creators). The Challenge Set was defined operationally: questions answered incorrectly by both the IR solver and the PMI solver were placed in the Challenge Set. A sample of 100 questions was manually categorized into knowledge types and reasoning types by the authors.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The partitioning into Challenge and Easy sets was done algorithmically using two baseline solvers (IR and PMI). The categorization of knowledge and reasoning types was based on a sample of 100 questions and required subjective judgement about the main challenge exhibited by different questions; the authors note that relative sizes of categories are necessarily approximate.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: IR solver using Elasticsearch (Waterloo corpus), PMI solver using pointwise mutual information on the Waterloo corpus, ElasticSearch for corpus indexing and retrieval, Open IE for structured representation extraction, AllenNLP framework for neural models.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The ARC Dataset, Corpus, three baseline neural models (DecompAttn, BiDAF, and DGEM), and a leaderboard are all publicly available at http://data.allenai.org/arc. A leaderboard is maintained for up-to-date results. Code is available at https://github.com/allenai/arc-solvers. No explicit versioning or deprecation policy is described.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to drive progress in AI research on advanced question answering, moving beyond factoid retrieval-style tasks toward questions requiring reasoning, commonsense knowledge, and deeper text comprehension. It is designed to encourage research on more difficult AI challenges rather than incremental improvements to simple retrieval algorithms.
rai:dataBiases: Questions vary in target student grade level (3rd to 9th grade), with substantial overlap in difficulty among grade levels. The dataset includes only non-diagram, multiple-choice science questions in English, limiting coverage to this domain and format. The ARC Corpus was found to be approximately 75% science-relevant based on informal analysis of a random sample of 805 documents. The Challenge Set definition is operationally tied to the specific IR and PMI algorithms used as filters, which may not perfectly capture all 'hard' questions.
rai:dataLimitations: The Challenge Set definition only approximates the informal goal of 'hard' questions, as it is defined by failure of two specific baseline algorithms. The ARC Corpus, while covering knowledge relevant to approximately 95% of Challenge questions, does not always contain direct answers; simple retrieval methods are insufficient to exploit the available knowledge. Only 11 question words (mainly proper nouns) do not appear in the ARC Corpus. The dataset contains only non-diagram, multiple-choice science questions in English, limiting generalizability. Some corpus similarities between the Waterloo corpus and ARC Corpus may affect IR solver scores.
rai:dataUseCases: Training, Testing, and Validation for question answering systems. The dataset is intended as a benchmark challenge for the AI research community to develop more advanced QA methods requiring reasoning, commonsense knowledge, and deeper text comprehension. Use of the ARC Corpus is optional; systems are not restricted to this corpus. The dataset is intended for non-commercial research purposes (at least for the Mercury question source).
